explanation: Mixture with no shared theme. It fires on the 'ores' of 'electrophoresis' after 'gel', on code tokens (esc_html, Import, Pool, debug, flyweight), on legal and institutional names (Anders v., Circuit Judge, Royal Astronomical Society) and on scattered words like 'blurted', 'warrant', 'otherwise'. The one repeated pattern is the end of 'gel electrophoresis'.

Polysemantic. It fires on the digit or hyphen inside legal docket numbers ('No. 93-3005', 'No. 96'), on separators in lists and keywords (commas, semicolons, 'and', 'e.g.'), on code type and method tokens (*FmtCtx, .new, *unicode) and on miscellaneous words in abstracts. Docket numbers are the clearest group.

Fires on word-piece tokens in the middle of words, mostly in non-English text (Finnish, Danish, French, Turkish, Portuguese, Hindi), in legal citations ('A.2d', 'Fed. Rep.', 'COMPLAINT', spaced-out 'O P I N I O N') and in odd strings such as a URL path. The token is a fragment inside a word or abbreviation rather than a whole common English word. Activations outside the top example are moderate.

Fires on words about sleep and bedtime: 'sleep' or 'sleeping' (strongest in phrases like 'side sleepers', 'go to sleep', 'put to sleep'), 'bed', 'night', 'slept', 'snuggled'. It fires more weakly on places for resting or lodging: hotel rooms, home, accommodation.

No clear theme. It fires on a mix of medical and disease word-pieces (cirrhosis, rabies, encephalopathy, vasculature, kidney), on function words ('y', 'for', 'across', 'to') and on assorted nouns in mostly scientific or formal prose. No token or context is shared across the examples.

Fires on nouns for the shape of a measured signal or statistical distribution in scientific text: 'distribution' (Maxwell-Boltzmann, normal, probability), 'curve(s)', 'spectrum/spectra', 'peak', 'maxima', 'broadened'. It also fires on 'of' in phrases like 'shape of' or 'section of' a curve.

Fires on function words and modifiers just before the main complement of an evaluative or quantitative phrase, e.g. 'for' in 'do it for money' or 'for several hours', 'leading' in 'one of the leading causes', 'oldest', 'most important', 'of' in 'drugs of abuse' or 'duration of'. This is common in medical and abstract prose. It is a weak syntactic pattern rather than a lexical one.

Mixture. It fires on mid-word fragments of rare or long words (sumptuous, rhinoceroses, precepts, hermaphroditism, Shandong, LUBBOCK, Japanese characters) and also on relative or function words after a noun ('while', 'where', 'who', 'which', 'for years'). The two groups are unrelated.

Fires mainly on tokens inside numbers, dates, IDs and algebra expressions (digits in prices, years, barcodes and dates, '*s' or '*g' variables in math problems, '/' in dates and URLs) and on foreign-key column names in SQL schemas (FK_ProfileId, resource_id). There are a few unrelated prose words ('theirs', 'share', 'are').

Mostly fires on word-piece continuations inside technical or rare words, e.g. 'decoder' or 'coder' in encoder-decoder, cystic 'fib'rosis, 'sc-int'igraphy, neoant'ig'ens, immun'ogenic', 'AP' in '(AP)' datelines, plus some unrelated phrase words ('following', 'Get', 'out'). It looks like a completion detector for familiar multi-token terms, but it is loose.

Fires on the 'ag' piece in 'coagulation' or 'coagulopathy' (strongest), on 'way' in 'all the way', and on the last word of set phrases ('come to life', 'modern-day', 'checkered flag', 'groups such as'). Overall it is a mixture of idiom completions and word-pieces.

No coherent theme. It fires on '(' after a person's full name in biography openings ('Jake Jones (November...'), on 'v.' in case captions, and on scattered pronouns, prepositions and nouns in many genres ('it', 'you', 'of', 'vaginal', 'configuration').

Fires at the start of a C/C++/Objective-C declaration or statement in code: keywords like 'enum', 'class', 'static', 'public', 'char' at the beginning of a line after a namespace or include block, and '[' starting an Objective-C message send ('= [NSOperationQueue new'). Boost or include path pieces fire moderately.

Fires on verbs, conjunctions and prepositions in news-headline-like or descriptive prose ('stuck', 'entering', 'described', 'reeling', 'installed', 'or', 'and', 'to', 'from'). No clear lexical or semantic theme ties them together.

Fires on the '(' that opens an acronym after a spelled-out name ('Growth hormone (GH)', 'Integration Host Factor (IHF)'), and also on fragments of IDs, usernames, numbers and proper names (GitHub handles, DOIs, database table names, species names). The acronym-parenthesis case is the strongest and most consistent.

Mixture. It fires on medical word-pieces (in'contin'ence, thromboemb'ol'ism, pro'gen'itor, Kaplan-Me'ier', T3'N'0M0), on legal citation pieces ('cv', 'B.R.', 'No. 02-', '501(c)') and on scattered words like 'gone', 'this', 'transfer'.

Fires on word-pieces and numbers inside dense biomedical abstracts (anticata'le'ptic, ret'ic'ulum, uter'ine', du'oden'alis, HT-108'0', E. coli K'-'12), and on pieces of legal captions and docket numbers, config keys and connection strings. It responds to subword tokens in technical, jargon-heavy text rather than to any meaning.

Fires on tokens in fixed boilerplate phrases ('contributor license agreements', 'list of conditions', 'distributed in the hope') and on words for amounts and units ('a few pixels/milliseconds', 'less than a million', 'terabytes'), plus 'rows and columns'. The two groups are unrelated.

Fires on the first piece of a proper name, citation or number after a lead-in (e.g. 'R' in 'Ratu', 'Ry' in 'Ryland', 'End' in 'St. Enda', digits after 'pgen.' or 'ppat.' in DOI-style citations, phone and race numbers) and on Japanese mid-word tokens. These have no shared meaning.

Fires on sports and fitness words: exercise and activity names (yoga poses, burpees, rock climbing, shot put, surfboard, backstroke, gymnastics), MMA terms (submission, flyweight), and training or sports-event nouns (agility, track, circuit, footwork, ring). Strongest on yoga or workout exercises.
